# Computer Arithmetic and Number Representation

Positional systems, the four conversion methods, the binary codes for decimal digits,
sign-magnitude and both complements, arithmetic performed inside a code, and IEEE-754 —
built from the field definitions rather than from the platform. Python 3.11+, no
dependencies, **1,844 tests**. A [[clean-room-rebuild-from-specification]] of the
first-semester Computer System Organization syllabus.

## Why rebuild what `int()` and `struct` already do

Because neither answers the question the material asks. `int("1010", 2)` returns ten without
saying whether it used Horner's scheme or formed the weights, and `struct.pack(">f", 0.1)`
returns four bytes without saying what was lost.

Both facts are recoverable only by writing the method out, which is
[[make-the-formal-object-observable]] applied to arithmetic: every conversion returns a
`Trace` holding the intermediate quotients and subtractions an exercise expects to see in the
margin, and the tests check the trace as well as the answer. A method that reaches the right
result by the wrong route has not been implemented.

## Closed forms, not ratio bands

[[counted-complexity-assertions]] taken one step further than the DSAA repository needed.
Direct method I forms every weight and costs `w(w−1)/2 + 2w`; Horner forms none and costs
`2w`. Both closed forms are asserted at five widths.

A ratio test was written first and discarded. The measured ratios are 3.14, 3.45 and 3.68 —
all short of the 4 a purely quadratic term would give, because the linear part still dominates
at these widths. A tolerance band loose enough to accept 3.14 would also accept a genuinely
linear implementation, which is [[tests-that-pass-for-the-wrong-reason]] in its most tempting
form: the test would have passed, and it would have been measuring nothing.

## A property that classifies, rather than a table to memorise

Four decimal codes are usually taught as four tables. Three share a property the fourth lacks —
see [[self-complementing-codes]] — and `is_self_complementing` computes it rather than
declaring it, so a code added later classifies correctly without a flag anyone has to remember
to set.

The correction counts follow from it and are measured over all 100 single-digit pairs per code:
BCD 8421 needs its plus-six on 45 of them, Aiken on 25 in **both directions**, Excess-3 on all
100 but unconditionally, with only the sign varying. The exercise sheet prints two examples.

## Two defects the range tests caught

Both passed the exercise sheet's own examples, which is the point.

**The p's complement of zero overflows its width.** Complementing `000` gives `1000`; the
leading digit falls off the fixed width and the carry it stood for went with it, so every
`a − 0` came back negative. The sheets contain no subtraction by zero. The 121-pair grid does.

**Aiken's code words were self-complementing and still wrong.** Two patterns satisfy the
constraint for digits 5 to 7 and the published code takes the higher one; taking the first
found produced a real self-complementing code that was not Aiken's — passing every round-trip
test and disagreeing with the textbook table.

Both are written up beside their fixes, following
[[document-the-failure-mode-next-to-the-fix]].

## The error is a number

Every figure is computed in `fractions.Fraction`, so the arithmetic that measures
floating-point error is not itself floating point. `0.1` encodes to `13421773 / 2²⁷` in
binary32 and the shortfall is stated exactly; `0.1 + 0.2 − 0.3` is exactly `2⁻⁵⁵`.

The IEEE-754 encoder is checked against `struct` in the useful direction only — an independent
implementation agreeing with the platform is evidence, whereas wrapping the platform and
comparing against itself would prove nothing. That is
{{reference-implementation-as-specification}} used as a cross-check rather than as a source.

## Verification

A 2026-08-12 local audit passed all 1,844 pytest cases. The audit set `PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT` to an
external writable temporary root because this sandbox cannot access the owner's Temp directory; that
